name: Rubric B (Balanced), tightened anchors
changeNote: Same criteria and weights as v1. Every level 0–4 is now defined with observable tests, edge cases are ruled on, and a tie-break rule is added, so the same CV scores the same way every time.
scoringRules: Score only what the CV text states. Job titles alone prove nothing: a level needs the described activity.
A level applies only when every condition in it is met. If any condition is missing, go down a level.
If the evidence sits between two levels, or you are unsure, choose the lower level.
Score each criterion on its own. Strength in one criterion never raises another.
Count activity from any job on the CV, including earlier non-product roles, unless the criterion says otherwise.
Internships and traineeships under 6 months count as exposure only (at most level 2 where the criterion allows).

criteria.name: Lived the operation

anchors.4: At least 1 year in a hands-on operational role at a logistics operator (freight forwarder, 3PL, customs broker/CHA, port or terminal, carrier, shipping line), doing operational work such as shipment execution, documentation, carrier coordination or exception handling; AND afterwards worked at a software company or in a product, engineering or tech role.
anchors.3: Either: at least 1 year of hands-on logistics operations as in level 4 but never moved to a software company or tech role. Or: at least 1 year in a commercial or client-facing role at a logistics operator (sales, account management) with direct operational involvement, followed by a move to a software company.
anchors.2: Under 1 year of hands-on logistics operations (internship, traineeship, rotation); or at least 1 year of operations in an adjacent operations-heavy field (e-commerce fulfilment, warehousing inside a non-logistics company, manufacturing, field operations, supply-chain planning).
anchors.1: Logistics only from the software or vendor side: built integrations with, sold software to, or supported logistics companies, without working in their operations.

criteria.notes: Consulting for logistics firms counts as operations only if the CV describes doing the operational work, not advising on it.

criteria.name: Owns the bad moment

anchors.4: Names a specific failure, loss or crisis (a named incident, not a category); says what they personally did; AND says how they closed it with the people affected (told customers, wrote or shared the post-mortem, ran the follow-up to closure).
anchors.3: Names a specific failure or crisis with real stakes for customers or operations, and what they personally did to resolve it, but nothing about closing the loop with the people affected.
anchors.2: Describes fixing a specific technical or process problem (a bug, an outage cause, a broken workflow) without customer or business stakes, or without it being their failure to own.
anchors.1: Only generic mentions of problems ("handled escalations", "resolved issues") with no specific incident.

criteria.notes: Killing a feature is not a failure for this criterion (it is scored under J1).

criteria.name: No one in between

anchors.4: The CV says they were the primary or direct contact for users, customers or operators as an ongoing part of a role ("primary contact", "owned the relationship", "worked directly with", sole PM running discovery with customers).
anchors.3: Regular hands-on contact with end users or customers themselves (ran their own customer sessions, worked on site with customers, handled customer accounts), but not stated as the primary contact.
anchors.2: Contact only through occasional structured research or interviews, or through other teams relaying customer input.
anchors.1: Indirect only: support tickets, analytics, surveys, reports from others.

criteria.notes: Internal stakeholders (their own engineering, sales or leadership teams) are not users. Carriers, agents and customs brokers count as operators when the candidate coordinated with them directly.

anchors.4: Most of the metrics they report are the customer's: tickets, churn, delays, errors, time-to-value, inspection or compliance results.
anchors.3: About half their metrics are the customer's.
anchors.2: At least one customer metric, but most are their own output.
anchors.1: Only their own output metrics, but at least one metric.

anchors.4: States they took on a larger load or a surge (more accounts, volume, scope) without extra headcount.
anchors.3: Covered for a departed colleague or ran two roles at once, stated explicitly.
anchors.2: Built a territory, function or area alone from scratch.
anchors.1: Handled a large load, without saying it grew or that headcount stayed flat.

criteria.name: Shipped, killed, measured

anchors.4: Shipped software features or products; AND explicitly killed, stopped or reversed at least one because of data (usage, adoption, results); AND reports measured outcomes of what they shipped.
anchors.3: Shipped software features with measured outcomes, and stopped or pivoted something, but without saying data drove it.
anchors.2: Shipped software features with at least one measured outcome; nothing killed.
anchors.1: Built something that is not a software product feature (a spreadsheet or BI dashboard, an internal process, a report), or shipped software with no measured outcome.

criteria.notes: Software features count whoever built them (PM, engineer, founder). Sales, customer success and operations roles score 1 at most unless the CV describes shipping software.

anchors.4: Owned integrations, APIs, data pipelines, data quality or build-vs-configure decisions end to end: they made the decisions and delivered.
anchors.3: Led the delivery of integration or data work where the key decisions sat with someone else, or owned one integration end to end.
anchors.2: Worked on integration, API or data work as a contributor on a team.
anchors.1: Used or configured integrated systems as a user or operator (TMS, ERP, EDI, customs portals), including onboarding clients onto a system.

criteria.name: Makes calls without a layer above

anchors.4: Was the sole owner of a product, area or function with no one above making those calls (sole PM, founder, first hire in the function), AND the CV names decisions they made.
anchors.3: Owned an area and describes making its key calls, with a manager above who was not making them day to day.
anchors.2: Owned a workstream or area inside a larger team where senior people set direction.
anchors.1: Executed with some latitude but describes no decisions of their own.

criteria.notes: Owning a sales territory, a book of accounts or a consulting engagement is at most 2: the product and company calls sit elsewhere.

anchors.4: Created a team practice (a template, process, review, ritual) that the CV says others adopted.
anchors.3: Created a team practice, adoption not stated.

weightRationale.P1: Strongest pattern. PM works daily inside freight operations.
weightRationale.P3: The PM runs customer discovery directly
weightRationale.J1: The PM JD asks for "shipped things, killed things"
weightRationale.J2: The SPM owns the integration and data layer
weightRationale.J3: The SPM is the most senior PM, with "no committee"
